chapter 1: introduction

overview

optical character recognition (ocr) is a technology used to convert printed or handwritten text images into machine-readable text. while ocr systems have achieved high accuracy for english and other widely used languages, there is still a lack of efficient ocr systems for regional languages such as kannada. kannada is a complex script with a large number of characters, modifiers, and compound formations. traditional ocr systems struggle to accurately recognize kannada text due to variations in fonts, handwriting styles, and image quality.

this project aims to develop a kannada ocr system using deep learning techniques, specifically the crnn (convolutional recurrent neural network) (research paper[1], https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7801919) architecture with ctc (connectionist temporal classification)(research paper[2],https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1143844.1143891) loss. the system takes word images as input and outputs the corresponding kannada text. the implementation is carried out using python and trained using google colab with gpu support. the dataset consists of labeled kannada word images which are preprocessed and used for training the model.

objectives
the primary objectives of this project are:

to design an intelligent kannada optical character recognition (ocr) system capable of accurately recognizing printed text from input images and converting it into machine-readable format.
to implement a robust deep learning-based crnn (convolutional recurrent neural network) architecture that combines convolutional layers for feature extraction and recurrent layers for sequence modeling.
to utilize connectionist temporal classification (ctc) loss for effective sequence prediction without requiring character-level segmentation or alignment in the training data.
to train the ocr model using a labeled kannada word image dataset and enable the system to learn complex character patterns, structures, and variations in fonts.


to design an evaluation mechanism for measuring model performance using metrics such as accuracy and loss, and to optimize the model through hyperparameter tuning and training improvements.
to build a scalable and efficient ocr system that can be extended for real-world applications such as document digitization, text extraction, and integration into intelligent systems.

purpose, scope, and applicability

purpose
the purpose of this project is to design and develop an intelligent kannada optical character recognition (ocr) system that can accurately convert text from images into machine-readable digital format. the system aims to provide an efficient solution for recognizing printed kannada text from scanned documents or images by leveraging deep learning techniques such as convolutional recurrent .
neural networks (crnn). it focuses on improving accuracy through preprocessing, sequence modeling, and optimized training, thereby enabling applications such as document digitization, text extraction, and automation in regional language processing.

scope
the project scope encompasses the following components:
image preprocessing module: processing of input images using grayscale conversion, resizing, and normalization to improve recognition accuracy.
dataset preparation: organizing labeled kannada word images with corresponding annotations for training the ocr model.
crnn model architecture: implementation of a deep learning model combining cnn for feature extraction and rnn for sequence prediction.
ctc-based prediction: using ctc loss for recognizing text sequences without requiring character-level segmentation.
model training: training the ocr system using kannada dataset and evaluating performance based on accuracy.


ocr output system: generating kannada text from input images for practical usage.
the current scope excludes handwritten text recognition, mobile application development, and large-scale deployment.
applicability
this system is applicable in a wide range of real-world scenarios:
document digitization: converting printed kannada books, newspapers, and documents into digital text format.
government and administrative use: processing official records, forms, and regional language documents efficiently.
educational applications: assisting students and teachers in accessing and digitizing kannada study materials.
library and archive management: digitizing old manuscripts and preserving historical kannada documents.

organization of major-project phase-1
this report is organized into the following chapters:
chapter 1 – introduction: provides the overview, objectives, purpose, scope, and applicability of the kannada ocr project.
chapter 2 – literature survey: reviews existing ocr techniques, identifies limitations, and presents the problem statement and proposed solution.
chapter 3 – requirement engineering: details software and hardware tools, system design, and functional requirements of the ocr system.
chapter 4 – project planning: covers the development phases, training process, and implementation methodology.
chapter 5 – applications and conclusion: discusses real-world applications of the ocr system and concludes the project.


chapter 2: literature survey

introduction

optical character recognition (ocr) systems have evolved significantly over recent years, transitioning from traditional rule-based approaches to advanced deep learning-based methods. however, achieving high accuracy for regional languages like kannada remains a major challenge due to complex character structures and limited datasets. this chapter surveys the relevant existing literature across three key technology domains that underpin this project: (1) image preprocessing techniques for text enhancement,
(2) deep learning models for text recognition such as cnn and rnn, and (3) sequence prediction methods using ctc loss.
summary of papers

paper 1: crnn for image-based sequence recognition
shi et al. (2016) proposed and evaluated a convolutional recurrent neural network (crnn) model(research paper[1], https://ieeexplore.ieee.org/document/7801919) for text recognition. the system combines convolutional layers for feature extraction and recurrent layers for sequence prediction. their evaluation demonstrated that crnn can achieve high accuracy without requiring character-level segmentation. the paper provides key insights into end-to-end ocr system design directly applicable to this project.

paper 2: connectionist temporal classification (ctc)
graves et al. (2006) presented a sequence labeling method using connectionist temporal classification (research paper[2],https://dl.acm.org/doi/10.1145/1143844.1143891)for unsegmented data. the authors applied recurrent neural networks to map input sequences directly to output labels. their work demonstrates that ctc enables accurate prediction without alignment between input and output. this validates the use of ctc loss in the proposed ocr system.
paper 3: attention-based scene text recognition
shi et al. (2017) proposed an attention-based model for scene text recognition using deep learning. the system integrates attention mechanisms with sequence modeling to improve accuracy. their findings


show that focusing on relevant parts of the image enhances recognition performance. this approach provides insights into improving ocr systems for complex text structures.

paper 4: tesseract ocr engine
smith (2007) developed and evaluated the tesseract ocr engine (research paper[4] , 10.1109/icdar.2007.4376991)for text recognition. the system uses pattern recognition and feature extraction techniques for converting images to text. their evaluation demonstrated good performance for standard printed text. however, limitations exist in handling complex scripts like kannada, motivating advanced deep learning approaches.

paper 5: paddleocr system

duetal. (2020) proposed a practical lightweight ocr system called paddleocr(https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.09941). the system leverages deep learning models for text detection and recognition across multiple languages. their evaluation demonstrated improved accuracy and efficiency in real-world scenarios. the paper provides insights into scalable ocr system development.

paper 6: deep text recognition benchmark
baek et al. (2019) presented a comprehensive benchmark for evaluating deep text recognition models. the authors compared multiple architectures and training techniques for ocr tasks. their study demonstrates the importance of model design and data preparation in achieving high accuracy. this work supports the selection of deep learning models for ocr systems.
paper 7: document image processing techniques
o’gorman and kasturi (1995) proposed various preprocessing techniques for document image analysis. the system focuses on noise removal, binarization, and normalization methods. their findings show that preprocessing significantly improves ocr performance. these techniques are directly applicable to improving input image quality in this project.




drawbacks of existing systems

analysis of existing ocr systems and related literature reveals the following key drawbacks:

low accuracy for regional languages: most ocr systems perform well for english but show poor accuracy for kannada due to complex character structures and limited datasets.
dependence on high-quality images: existing systems require clear and high-resolution images, making them less effective for blurred, noisy, or low-quality inputs.
difficulty in handling complex characters: kannada script contains compound characters and modifiers, which are difficult for traditional ocr systems to recognize accurately.
limited dataset availability: there is a lack of large, well-annotated kannada datasets, which affects the training and performance of ocr models.
segmentation issues: many traditional ocr systems rely on character segmentation, which becomes challenging for connected or overlapping text.
lack of robust preprocessing: inadequate preprocessing techniques lead to poor feature extraction and reduced overall recognition performance.

problem statement

existing ocr systems often struggle to accurately recognize kannada text due to the complexity of the script and limited availability of high-quality datasets. in situations such as low-resolution images, varying fonts, noisy backgrounds, and complex character combinations, traditional ocr methods fail to produce reliable results, making text extraction inefficient and error-prone.

furthermore, no existing widely deployed solution effectively combines: (a) advanced image preprocessing techniques, (b) deep learning-based sequence modeling using crnn, and (c) alignment-free prediction using ctc loss for kannada text recognition. this gap constitutes the core problem this project addresses.


proposed solution

this project proposes a kannada optical character recognition (ocr) system that operates as follows:

the input image containing kannada text is first preprocessed using techniques such as grayscale conversion, resizing, and normalization to enhance image quality.
the preprocessed image is passed through a convolutional neural network (cnn) to extract meaningful visual features.
the extracted features are then processed using a recurrent neural network (rnn) to learn sequential dependencies in the text.
connectionist temporal classification (ctc) loss is applied to predict the final text sequence without requiring character-level segmentation.
the predicted output is decoded to generate readable kannada text, which can be used for further applications such as digitization and text processing.

the solution is deep learning-based, efficient, scalable, and designed to accurately recognize kannada text from images under varying conditions.

conceptual / analysis modeling

the following uml diagrams describe the system architecture and dynamic behaviour of the kannada optical character recognition (ocr) system.



use case diagram
the use case diagram identifies the primary actors and their interactions with the system. the two main actors are the user (who uploads or provides the input image) and the ocr system (which processes the image and generates text output). a third optional actor is the administrator (who manages dataset, model training, and system configuration).

sequence diagram
the sequence diagram describes the interaction between components over time for the primary use case: image input → text recognition → output display.
sequence of events:

ocr system preprocesses the image (resize, grayscale, normalization).

output.

→ end

software requirements specification

user requirements
functional requirements (from user perspective):

chapter 4: project planning

project planning and scheduling

the project follows an iterative and incremental development methodology. given that the system involves multiple interdependent components—image preprocessing, dataset preparation, deep learning model (crnn), and sequence prediction using ctc—development is planned in well-defined phases to allow for continuous training, testing, and performance improvement.

m3: crnn model implementation and initial training completed with baseline accuracy (week 12) m4: improved model performance through training optimization and parameter tuning (week 16) m5: implementation of ctc-based sequence prediction and text decoding (week 18)
m6: end-to-end ocr system testing with accurate kannada text recognition (week 20) m7: final system demonstration and report submission (week 26)

chapter 5: applications and conclusion

applications

the kannada optical character recognition (ocr) system is broadly applicable across numerous real-world scenarios where efficient text extraction and digitization are required.

document digitization
the system enables users to convert printed kannada books, newspapers, and documents into digital text format. this helps in preserving important information and making it easily accessible for storage, search, and editing purposes.
government and administrative applications
in government offices, large volumes of kannada documents and records need to be processed regularly. this system allows automatic extraction of text from forms and files, reducing manual effort and improving efficiency.
educational applications
students and teachers can use the system to digitize study materials, notes, and question papers. it helps in converting printed kannada content into editable and searchable digital format for learning purposes.
translation and language processing
the ocr system can be integrated with translation tools to convert kannada text into other languages. this enables better communication and accessibility of regional content across different platforms.
library and archive management
libraries and archives can use the system to digitize old manuscripts and historical kannada documents. this helps in preserving cultural heritage and making rare documents available in digital form.
business and automation applications
organizations can use ocr to automate data entry from invoices, receipts, and printed forms. this reduces human effort, minimizes errors, and improves overall workflow efficiency.


conclusion

this project proposes and implements a kannada optical character recognition (ocr) system designed to address the challenges of accurately recognizing regional language text from images. by combining image preprocessing techniques with deep learning models such as convolutional recurrent neural networks (crnn) and ctc-based sequence prediction, the system provides an efficient and reliable solution for text extraction.

the project has successfully completed dataset preparation, preprocessing, and model implementation phases. the trained model demonstrates the ability to recognize kannada text from word images and convert it into machine-readable format. this implementation serves as a strong foundation for further improvements and real-world applications.

the subsequent enhancements can include improving model accuracy with larger datasets, supporting handwritten text recognition, and integrating the system into mobile or web applications. the innovation of this project lies in its use of deep learning techniques for regional language processing, enabling more accurate and scalable ocr solutions.
upon completion, the system is expected to provide a practical and efficient framework for kannada text recognition applicable across document digitization, education, translation systems, and automation in various domains.

from .models import student, course 
from .forms import studentregistrationform , courseselectionform  
 
def register_student (request): 
    if request.method == 'post': 
        form = studentregistrationform (request.post) 
        if form.is_valid (): 
            student = form.save() 
            return redirect ('select_course' , student_id =student.id) 
    else: 
        form = studentregistrationform () 
    return render(request, 'courses/register_student.html' , {'form': form}) 
 
def select_course (request, student_id ):

student = get_object_or_404 (student, id=student_id ) 
    if request.method == 'post': 
        form = courseselectionform (request.post) 
        if form.is_valid (): 
            course = form.cleaned_data ['course' ] 
            course.students.add( student) 
            return redirect ('course_students' , course_id =course.id) 
    else: 
        form = courseselectionform () 
    return render(request, 'courses/select_course.html' , {'form': form, 
'student' : student}) 
 
def course_students (request, course_id ): 
    course = get_object_or_404 (course, id=course_id ) 
    students  = course.students .all() 
    return render(request, 'courses/course_students.html' , {'course' : course, 
'students' : students })

introduction
deepak d, asst. prof., dept. of cse, canara engg. college 3artificial neural networks (anns) provide a general, practical method
for learning real-valued, discrete-valued, and vector-valued target
functions from examples.

biological motivation
•the study of artificial neural networks (anns) has been inspired by the
observation that biological learning systems are built of very complex webs of
interconnected neurons
•human information processing system consists of brain neuron: basic building
block cell that communicates information toand from various parts of body
•simplest model of a neuron: considered asa threshold unit –a processing element
(pe)
•collects inputs & produces output ifthe sum ofthe input exceeds aninternal
threshold value

deepak d, asst. prof., dept. of cse, canara engg. college 20•a prototypical example ofann learning isprovided bypomerleau's ( 1993 )
system alvinn, which uses a learned ann tosteer anautonomous vehicle
driving atnormal speeds on public highways.
•theinput tothe neural network isa 30x32 grid of pixel intensities obtained from
a forward-pointed camera mounted on the vehicle.
•the network output isthe direction inwhich the vehicle issteered.

deepak d, asst. prof., dept. of cse, canara engg. college 21•figure illustrates the neural network representation.
•the network isshown on the left side of the figure, with the input camera image
depicted below it.
•each node (i.e., circle) inthe network diagram corresponds tothe output ofa
single network unit, and the lines entering the node from below are itsinputs.
•there are four units that receive inputs directly from all of the 30 x 32 pixels in
the image. these are called "hidden" units because their output isavailable only
within the network and isnotavailable aspartofthe global network output. each
of these four hidden units computes a single real-valued output based on a
weighted combination of its960 inputs
•these hidden unit outputs are then used asinputs toa second layer of 30 "output"
units.
•each output unit corresponds toa particular steering direction, and the output
values of these units determine which steering direction isrecommended most
strongly.

deepak d, asst. prof., dept. of cse, canara engg. college 22•the diagrams on the right side of the figure depict the learned weight values 
associated with one of the four hidden units in this ann. 
•the large matrix of  black and white boxes on the lower right depicts the weights 
from the 30 x 32 pixel inputs into the hidden unit. here, a white box indicates a 
positive weight, a black box a negative weight, and the size of the box indicates 
the weight magnitude.
•the smaller rectangular diagram directly above the large matrix shows the 
weights from this hidden unit to each of the 30 output units.

appropriate problems for 
neural network learning
ann is appropriate for problems with the following characteristics : 
•instances are represented by many attribute-value pairs.
•the target function output may be discrete-valued, real-valued, or a vector of
several real- or discrete-valued attributes.
•thetraining examples may contain errors.
•long training times are acceptable.
•fast evaluation of the learned target function may be required
•theability of humans tounderstand the learned target function isnot important
deepak d, asst. prof., dept. of cse, canara engg. college 23

architectures of artificial neural networks
anartificial neural network canbedivided into three parts (layers), which are
known as:
•input layer: this layer isresponsible for receiving information (data), signals,
features, or measurements from the external environment. these inputs are usually
normalized within the limit values produced by activation functions
•hidden, intermediate, or invisible layers: these layers are composed of neurons
which are responsible for extracting patterns associated with the process or system
being analysed. these layers perform most of the internal processing from a
network.
•output layer : this layer isalso composed ofneurons, and thus isresponsible for
producing and presenting the final network outputs, which result from the
processing performed by the neurons inthe previous layers.
deepak d, asst. prof., dept. of cse, canara engg. college 24

architectures of artificial neural networks
the main architectures of artificial neural networks, considering the neuron
disposition, how they are interconnected and how itslayers are composed, canbe
divided asfollows:
1. single-layer feedforward network
2.multi-layer feedforward networks
3. recurrent or feedback networks
4.mesh networks

single-layer feedforward architecture
•this artificial neural network has just one input layer and a single neural layer, which isalso the
output layer.
•figure illustrates a simple-layer feedforward network composed ofn inputs and m outputs.
•the information always flows ina single direction (thus, unidirectional), which isfrom the input
layer tothe output layer
deepak d, asst. prof., dept. of cse, canara engg. college 26

multi-layer feedforward architecture
•this artificial neural feedforward networks with multiple layers are composed of one or more
hidden neural layers.
•figure shows a feedforward network with multiple layers composed ofoneinput layer with n
sample signals, two hidden neural layers consisting ofn1and n2neurons respectively, and, finally,
oneoutput neural layer composed ofm neurons representing the respective output values ofthe
problem being analyzed.
deepak d, asst. prof., dept. of cse, canara engg. college 27

recurrent or feedback architecture
•inthese networks, the outputs ofthe neurons are used asfeedback inputs for other neurons.
•figure illustrates an example of a perceptron network with feedback, where one of its output 
signals is fed back to the middle layer.

•a perceptron takes a vector of real-valued inputs, calculates a linear combination

otherwise

what setof functions can be represented by feed-forward networks?
